title: MEGA lab: interpreting bootstrap support on bacterial 16S rRNA
summary: Read bootstrap support as a count of replicate trees on the 27-sequence bacterial 16S rRNA alignment — MEGA's NJ chain under K2P and pairwise deletion — comparing two seeded NeoPhylo runs and MEGA-CC 12.1.4's recorded 100- and 1,000-replicate runs, then reading the `*` weak marker on the weak-support sample.

prompts.concept: The NJ run's last join: past it the finished tree is an unrooted NJ tree — on a UPGMA run this position is still mid-run, two of its 26 merges remain. Read the finished tree by its groupings — the two enteric bacteria together (Escherichia with Salmonella); the two mollicutes together (Mycoplasmoides with Spiroplasma); the two cyanobacteria together (Nostoc with Synechococcus); the Deinococcus–Thermus pair; a Bacillus–Staphylococcus firmicute pair; and an alphaproteobacterial triple (Agrobacterium, Caulobacter and Rickettsia). Each is one grouping the bootstrap counts: how many of the resampled trees rebuild it?
prompts.math: Every internal edge of an unrooted tree defines a split; a replicate resamples the kept columns, rebuilds the distance matrix and the NJ tree, and a grouping's support is the share of the replicate trees whose split sets contain it.

prompts.concept: Before you run, make a prediction: which internal branch of the inferred tree will the data support least? Click that branch — terminal branches don't count — then run the bootstrap.
prompts.math: Each replicate resamples the kept columns with replacement, rebuilds the distance matrix and the NJ tree; a grouping's support is the share of the successful replicate trees whose split sets contain it.
prompts.reveal: The weakest grouping sits where the data's signal is thinnest — a grouping whose evidence a resample can miss entirely. A low count means this alignment says little about that spot — not that the grouping is wrong.

prompts.concept: Each label is a count — of the run's replicate trees that rebuilt that grouping — never a probability that the grouping is true. The `*` and the thinner branch mark a grouping under 50 — NeoPhylo's own flag for 'fewer than half the replicates', a reading aid, not a verdict. If you have not yet, do the handout's step 6: change the Seed and run again — same data, same settings, so the tree's groupings cannot move; only the counts can.

Two runs of the same analysis are two samples of the same resampling — whenever the resamples differ, the counts can move; the tree's groupings never do at the same settings. The handout's step 7 has you compare the counts MEGA's unseeded samples produce at two replicate sizes. Its step 8 then opens the second dataset in the sandbox.

lab.title: MEGA: Interpreting bootstrap support on 16S rRNA
objectives: Run MEGA's NJ bootstrap chain on a 27-taxon bacterial 16S rRNA alignment and read each support as a count of replicate trees — never a probability
Tell sampling noise from the analysis itself: two seeded NeoPhylo runs, and MEGA's recorded runs at 100 and at 1,000 replicates on the same data

lab.handout_md:
## What this lab reads

This lab runs one MEGA chain — the first run of the 100-replicates handout: a Neighbor-Joining tree on Kimura 2-parameter distances with the bootstrap test of phylogeny, under pairwise deletion — and its subject is what the support numbers mean: what they count, what they cannot tell you, and how far two runs of the same analysis can disagree while meaning the same thing. The recorded values are MEGA-CC 12.1.4's own — a 100-replicate run and a 1,000-replicate run on the same alignment.

## The data

Two datasets. The first is the 27-sequence bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA alignment the previous handout used — one genus each, over 1,628 aligned sites with real indels: pairwise deletion removes no column — all 1,628 stay in the alignment, but each pair is compared only over the sites where neither of the two has a gap or missing base (complete deletion keeps the 1,199 columns where all 27 sequences carry a base — that was the previous handout's second run). The sequences are NCBI RefSeq records aligned with MAFFT, bundled as the `16s-rrna` library dataset.

The second is the weak-support example: six sequences A–F over 120 sites, simulated in-house so that at least one grouping draws weak support. There is no recorded MEGA run for it — the last steps are a NeoPhylo-only read of weak support on NeoPhylo's own display, never a MEGA comparison and never a number to match.

To cross-check the 16S runs in MEGA itself: load this lab, export the alignment as `.meg` from NeoPhylo's Export menu, open that file in MEGA, and apply the settings table exactly — once at 100 replicates, once at 1,000.

## Before you start

Read the settings table. In MEGA the run's options live in the analysis dialog you reach from the menu path in the second column; the table lists every option the runs set — nothing is left to a default — next to the NeoPhylo control that reproduces it. The 1,000-replicate row is MEGA's second recorded run — you perform it in MEGA only; on the NeoPhylo side a second seeded run makes the same point and is much faster. And the seed row has no MEGA counterpart: MEGA's bootstrap is unseeded — every MEGA run is a fresh sample — while NeoPhylo's Seed is what makes your run reproducible.

## Steps

1. Load this lab. NeoPhylo loads the 16S alignment and computes the K80 matrix — MEGA's "Kimura 2-parameter" — under pairwise deletion.
2. Step through the joins (or jump to the end) and read the finished tree as a set of groupings — every internal branch is one claim about the data, and the bootstrap counts how many resampled trees rebuild each.
3. Before you run, the prompt asks for a prediction: click the internal branch you expect the data to support least — terminal branches don't count.
4. Run the bootstrap at the table's settings — MEGA's Test of Phylogeny: Bootstrap method at 100 replicates. Each label that lands on an internal branch is a count of the run's replicate trees.
5. Read the labels. A `*` next to a count marks a grouping under 50 — NeoPhylo's flag for "fewer than half the replicates", a reading aid, not a verdict. Open "Watch one replicate" to see what one count is made of: one resample of the columns and the NJ tree rebuilt from it, side by side with yours.
6. Change the Seed — any other value — and run again. Same data, same settings: your two runs are two samples of the same resampling, so the tree's groupings cannot move — only the counts can.
7. In MEGA: open the exported `.meg` and run the chain at the table's 100-replicate settings, then again at 1,000 replicates. MEGA labels the same original tree at both counts — the replicate number never re-picks the tree — so compare the counts: where did they move between your two MEGA runs, and between MEGA's and yours?
8. The last part is NeoPhylo-only — there is no recorded MEGA run for the second dataset. Switch to the Sandbox (the Lesson | Sandbox switch keeps the lab), and in the Import data section click "Weak-support example (DNA)" under "Paste or upload sequences, or try a sample:" — the six-taxon sample takes the sandbox over; nothing is saved or lost.
9. Step to the end of the sample's tree and run the bootstrap — the panel keeps your 100 replicates and a seed. Which groupings, if any, draw a `*` on this tree? Where one does, what does its low count say — and not say — about the grouping it flags? "Back to the lesson" returns to the lab; it asks before the sample is cleared.

## Questions

- Say it precisely: a support is the percent of replicate trees in which the grouping appeared — never a probability that the grouping is true, and not a statement about which tree is right. What exactly did each count on your tree measure?
- Low support is not a wrong grouping — the tree must put every taxon somewhere, and a grouping most replicates miss can still be the data's best answer. High support is not a true one either: a systematic error — a wrong model, unrepresentative taxa or sites — resamples the same wrong signal every replicate. Which of the 16S groupings would you defend as well supported, and on what grounds?
- Between your two seeded runs, which counts moved most? Between MEGA's 100- and 1,000-replicate runs the groupings never moved — how do the counts' moves compare at the two sizes, and what does that say about reading a count gathered from 100 replicates?
- The `*` flags a grouping under 50. In this lab's recorded MEGA runs two groupings sit under 50 at both replicate counts and a third sits just over. How many `*` does your first run show, and on which of MEGA's groupings do they fall? After your second seed, did any flag appear or vanish? Is a flag on a count near 50 a property of the data or of the draw — and what would change your mind about a flagged grouping?

lab.mega_note_md:
MEGA's Tree Explorer draws the inferred NJ tree with support printed as a percent on each internal branch — a count of how many of the run's replicate trees contain that grouping. Its Newick export writes the same supports as proportions to four decimals (`0.9800` where the screen showed 98; at 1,000 replicates a tenth of a point shows through, as `0.9720`); NeoPhylo shows the percent on the branch and writes integer percents (`98`) in its own Newick export.

MEGA's bootstrap labels the inferred tree — the grouping set is the data's NJ answer at the run's settings, never a resample's — so its 100- and 1,000-replicate runs label the same groupings and only the counts are samples. MEGA's bootstrap has no seed, so every MEGA run is a fresh sample and its counts move run to run; NeoPhylo's Seed makes your run reproducible, but it is its own sample, never MEGA's — two samples agree only within sampling noise.

NeoPhylo adds a convention of its own on top of the shared percent: a grouping under 50 draws a `*` next to its count and a thinner branch — NeoPhylo's flag for "fewer than half the replicates" — a display convention, not a significance test; MEGA's tree shows the bare percent. In this lab's two recorded MEGA runs two groupings sit under 50 at both replicate counts, and a third sits just over 50 each time. A count near 50 can land on either side of it between samples, so a flag on such a grouping is a property of that sample, not of the data.
